label: Functions on a Variety
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 237 through 296 and studies the functions that live on a variety. The coordinate ring records polynomial functions modulo those that vanish, and the field of rational functions captures quotients defined off a smaller set, turning geometry into the algebra of these function rings.

label: The Coordinate Ring
notes: The coordinate ring of a variety is the polynomial ring modulo the ideal of functions vanishing on it. Its elements are the polynomial functions on the variety, with two polynomials identified when they agree everywhere. This quotient ring encodes the variety's geometry algebraically and is reduced when the ideal is radical.

label: Polynomial Mappings
notes: A polynomial map between varieties is given in coordinates by polynomials and induces, by composition, a ring homomorphism between coordinate rings in the opposite direction. This contravariant correspondence makes geometry and algebra into mirror categories, with isomorphic varieties having isomorphic coordinate rings.

label: Quotient Rings and Remainders
notes: Computing in the coordinate ring means computing modulo the ideal, which a Grobner basis makes effective: each class has a canonical remainder under division by the basis. The standard monomials, those not divisible by any leading term, form a vector-space basis for the quotient ring.

label: Rational Functions
notes: On an irreducible variety the coordinate ring is a domain, so we may form its field of fractions, the field of rational functions. A rational function is defined wherever its denominator is nonzero, and its domain is an open dense subset of the variety.

label: Rational Maps
notes: Rational maps are given by rational functions and are defined on a dense open set, composing only where domains overlap. Varieties that are birationally equivalent share the same function field, a coarser and powerful notion of equivalence. Next: applications to robotics and theorem proving.
